title: India's Corporate Bond Market Just Had Its Biggest Week in Months. Borrowing Costs Fell 45 Basis Points in Five Days.
excerpt: Bajaj Finance, Muthoot, NABARD and a string of NBFCs are rushing to lock in cheap debt after the RBI's dollar measures triggered a sharp rally in short-term bonds.
body:
Indian companies raised more than 310 billion rupees — $3.24 billion — through bonds of up to five years in a single week, a pace that equals one-third of everything raised in the preceding two months combined. The rush was triggered by the Reserve Bank of India's measures to draw dollars into the country, which had an unexpected side effect: they crushed domestic borrowing costs.

The mechanics of the rally

Corporate bond yields for AAA-rated borrowers dropped 40 to 45 basis points in just five days, according to LSEG benchmark data. The spread over government bonds narrowed sharply. Before the RBI's announcement, yields had climbed to their highest levels in seven years as the Iran war drove up inflation expectations and foreign investors fled.

The turnaround was swift. When the RBI offered banks a subsidised swap window for overseas borrowings and fully absorbed hedging costs on NRI deposits, it gave lenders access to cheaper foreign currency funding. Some of that money flowed into short-term government bonds, pulling yields down. The rest signalled to the market that the central bank was serious about easing financial conditions even without cutting interest rates.

"A rise in overseas borrowings could reduce the need for local debt supply, leading to a rally in bonds below five years," said Ajay Marwaha, head of fixed income markets at Nuvama, a global wealth firm.

Who is borrowing

State-run institutions moved first. REC, the infrastructure finance company, raised three-year funds at a coupon of 7.34 per cent — significantly below secondary market levels. NABARD, which finances rural development, raised money at the same rate after having cancelled a similar issue in May when rates were approaching 8 per cent.

The private sector followed. Bajaj Finance has lined up issuances of 85 billion rupees. Muthoot Finance, India's largest gold lender, is raising 27.5 billion rupees. Bajaj Housing Finance and L&T Finance are each tapping the market for 15 to 20 billion rupees.

The common thread: all are non-banking financial companies that rely on wholesale funding and are acutely sensitive to movements in short-term rates. A 45-basis-point drop in borrowing costs translates directly into wider margins and cheaper loans for their own customers.

The yield curve is steepening

The rally has been concentrated in bonds with maturities of two to five years, led by the 6.36 per cent 2031 government bond, which has attracted about $500 million in foreign purchases over the past three days alone.

The gap between five-year and ten-year yields has widened to a one-year high of 40 basis points — more than double its pre-policy level. That steepening reflects a market that expects the short end to stay supported by the RBI's inflow measures while the long end remains exposed to global risks, fiscal dynamics and the possibility of rate hikes later this year.

"The short to medium end of the curve currently offers a more favourable risk-reward trade-off compared to the longer end," said Ashwin Patni, head of wealth management solutions at Julius Baer India.

The Bloomberg index question

Lurking in the background is a decision that could dwarf this week's moves. Bloomberg Index Services deferred India's inclusion in its flagship Global Aggregate bond index in January, citing operational concerns, and said it would provide an update by mid-2026.

India's finance minister has since met with RBI officials specifically to push for inclusion. The recent tax exemptions — scrapping withholding and capital gains taxes on foreign investments in government bonds — were partly designed to remove the operational barriers that Bloomberg had flagged.

If India is added to the index, passive tracking funds could bring $20 to $30 billion in new inflows over the inclusion period, similar to what happened when India entered JPMorgan's emerging market debt index in June 2024.

"These changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets.

What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs, the bond market rally has immediate and practical implications. Lower corporate borrowing costs translate into cheaper home loans, auto loans and business credit in India. NRI fixed deposit rates, which have risen above 7 per cent thanks to the RBI's FCNR subsidies, are now competing with a bond market that is offering some of the best risk-adjusted returns in years.

The broader signal is that India's credit markets are absorbing the oil shock faster than the equity markets suggest. While the Sensex is still down 13 per cent this year and foreign equity outflows have hit a record $30 billion, the debt side of the market is telling a different story — one of institutional confidence, policy responsiveness and capital flowing in rather than out.
